samples.text:
Nowadays smartphones are part of everyday life, even for children. Some people think that children should have their own phone when they start school, but others believe they should wait until they become teenager. I will discuss both sides and give my own opinion.

There are some reasons why parents give phones to young children. The main reason is safety. If a child has a phone, parents can call them anytime and know where they are, especially when they walk to school alone. In addition, smartphones have many educational apps which can help children to learn maths or reading in an interesting way. Some parents also think that if all other children in the class has a phone, their child will feel left out without one.

However, many people think young children are too young for smartphones. Firstly, spending a lot of time on screen is bad for children's eyes and it can reduce the time they spend playing outside or sleeping. Secondly, children cannot protect themself on the internet. They might see violent videos or talk to strangers without understand the danger. Moreover, phones can be very addictive and children may lose the concentration in class.

In my opinion, children should not have their own smartphone until they are teenagers. For safety, parents can give them a simple phone that can only make calls and send messages. When they are older, they are more responsible and parents can teach them how to use internet safely.

In conclusion, smartphones have some benefits for young children, like safety and learning, but the dangers are more serious. So I believe it is better for children to wait until teenage years before they get a smartphone.

samples.text:
Deciding when a child should receive their first smartphone has become a common dilemma for modern parents. Some argue that phones should be given as soon as children start school, while others feel they should be delayed until the teenage years. In my view, the latter approach is wiser, although a basic phone may be useful earlier.

Those who favour giving smartphones at a young age usually stress safety and convenience. A phone allows parents to contact their children at any time and, with location-sharing apps, to know exactly where they are. This can be particularly reassuring for working parents whose children travel to school or activities independently. Supporters also point out that many educational apps make learning interactive and enjoyable, and that children who grow up with technology will be better prepared for a digital world.

Nevertheless, there are serious concerns about young children owning such devices. Smartphones are designed to hold attention, and a six-year-old has limited ability to control how long they spend on games or videos. Excessive screen time is widely linked to poor sleep, reduced physical activity and difficulty concentrating. In addition, young children are poorly equipped to recognise online risks, such as inappropriate content or contact from strangers, and parental controls are rarely fool proof.

In my opinion, the risks for young children clearly outweigh the benefits. The safety argument is valid, but it can be met with a simple phone that only makes calls and sends texts. By the early teenage years, children are more mature, and parents can gradually introduce a smartphone with clear rules and open conversations about responsible use.

In conclusion, while early smartphone ownership offers some practical advantages, I believe children should generally wait until they are teenagers, using a basic phone in the meantime if they needs to stay in contact with their parents.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both sides extended and supported · logical organisation with clear paragraph topics · good collocations (screen time, online risks) · mostly accurate complex sentences with two minor slips.

samples.text:
The age at which children should be given a smartphone is a question that divides parents and educators. One view is that a child should have their own device from the first day of school; the opposing view is that ownership should be postponed until adolescence. While both positions reflect genuine concern for children's welfare, I believe that delaying full smartphone access is the more responsible course.

Advocates of early ownership frame the issue in terms of security and preparation. A smartphone enables parents to stay in touch with their children throughout the day and to track their location, which offers considerable peace of mind. There is also an argument that digital literacy is now as fundamental as reading, and that children who become familiar with technology early will navigate it more competently later. Finally, some parents fear that a child without a phone will be socially isolated if most classmates already own one.

Those who favour waiting, however, raise concerns that are harder to dismiss. Young children lack the self-discipline to limit their own screen time, and devices engineered to maximise engagement can easily displace sleep, outdoor play and face-to-face interaction, all of which are vital for healthy development. Equally worrying is children's vulnerability online: a seven-year-old is unlikely to recognise manipulative content or the risks of communicating with strangers, and even well-configured parental controls can be circumvented.

Weighing these arguments, I am persuaded that the risks of early ownership outweigh its advantages. The legitimate need for contact can be met by a basic handset without internet access, and digital skills can be taught under supervision at school or at home. Once children reach their early teens, a smartphone can be introduced gradually, with agreed limits that are relaxed as they demonstrate responsibility.

In conclusion, although giving young children smartphones offers reassurance and convenience, these benefits can be achieved in safer ways. Postponing ownership until the teenage years allows children to develop the maturity they need to use such devices wisely.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly developed and weighed · well-reasoned opinion with practical alternatives · seamless cohesion and logical sequencing · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of accurate complex structures.
